name: Uma Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and on Ridgeway Farm by five, bringing the cows in for milking. It's the Okafor family's place, about 120 milkers, plus barley and a field of kale for winter feed. I scrape the yard, wash down the parlour, feed the calves, and in the afternoon I'm on whatever job Mr Okafor's son, Femi, gives me, which this week was mending fence on the top field. I like the calves best. What wears me out is the cold water and the fact that I'm still slower than everyone at everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been farming, and what did you do before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I did fourteen years in the kitchen at the primary school, until the council handed the catering to a big contractor and they cut half of us. My grandad had cows, so I thought, why not. Gareth, my partner, drives the number 9 bus, and we've got Mia, who's thirteen, and Tom, who's ten. I'm forty-three and still the new girl, which is a funny place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I told you so. At the union meeting in the Plough last month a man from head office was going on about robots like the sky was falling. I'd tell the lads at work it was all talk, same as every other gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, because I've already lost one job to people in suits with a plan. If nothing really changes, I get to keep learning this one at my own pace. I'm not quick, I know that, but I get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up at five and keep asking Femi to show me the tractor jobs I'm still nervous on. I'd keep paying my union dues, eleven a month, because the other fights don't go away just because the robots did. Maybe finally get my pesticide certificate in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weight I didn't know I was carrying got put down. Not happy exactly, just normal, and normal is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good day in the parlour look like for you, if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be in the parlour at five with cold hands, and for once that sounds lovely. People think farm work is all fresh air, but it's mostly wet sleeves and cows treading on your boots. I'd take that over the alternative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything still worry you, even with AI fizzling out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Low pay, mostly, and the supermarkets squeezing the milk price so Mr Okafor can't pay any of us more. That's who I'd still be angry at. AI being hype doesn't fix that.

S0.say: I'd tell people it was hype all along and that I'd said so at the union meeting. I'd tell the lads at work it was all talk, like every other gadget.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I've already lost one job to someone else's plan. If nothing changes I get to keep learning this one at my own pace.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, turning up at five and asking her supervisor to teach her the tractor jobs. Keeps paying her union dues and plans to take her pesticide certificate in the spring.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a weight she didn't know she was carrying was put down.
S0.quote: I'd still be in the parlour at five with cold hands, and for once that sounds lovely.
S0.fieldNote: Uma's sense of threat comes from her last job, not from technology itself: she lost a school kitchen job to outsourcing and sees AI through that lens. Even in the mildest picture her anger stays aimed at supermarkets and milk prices. She's open about being slow to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same old story: they bring in machines and call it progress, and it's people like us who pay. I'd say it at the union branch and probably in the family group chat, which Gareth says I shouldn't. I'd want the government to make the companies pay for whoever they push out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ridgeway already has one robot milking unit on trial in the end shed, and the cows go to it on their own. If Femi gets two more, that's my mornings gone. I'm the newest, so I'm the first one they don't need. Nobody would say it to my face, but I'd know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask Femi straight out what his plans are, because I'd rather know. I'd push to get two or three months' wages saved instead of the six weeks we've got now, so no takeaway on Fridays and no new trainers for Tom till spring. And I'd bring it up at the branch, get the union to ask for a deal on how robots come in, with notice and a payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like a noise in the engine you can't place. I'm not losing sleep yet, but I'd catch myself watching that robot in the end shed when I should be working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your mornings in the parlour went, would you look for something else on the farm or leave farming altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in farming if they'd let me, because I've only just started being any good. People keep saying retrain, but I'm forty-three and I've already retrained once. You can only start over so many times before you're just starting over for a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of these AI tools yourself, to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. I've never even used one of those chat things, and I don't want to. Mia does her homework with it and I tell her to use her own head.

S1.say: I'd say it's the same old story, machines called progress and people like us paying for it. I'd want the government to make the companies pay for whoever gets pushed out.
S1.think: The robot milker already on trial in the end shed could take her mornings if two more come. She's the newest hire, so she'd expect to go first.
S1.do: Asks her boss directly about his plans for robot milkers. Cuts takeaways and new clothes to build savings from six weeks towards two or three months, and raises it at her union branch to push for notice and payouts.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an engine noise she can't place. She isn't losing sleep but keeps watching the robot milker.
S1.quote: You can only start over so many times before you're just starting over for a living.
S1.fieldNote: There's a concrete trigger in her life already: a robot milker on trial at Ridgeway. She refuses to try AI tools herself and won't retrain again, so her plan is to dig in, save and organise. Her line about starting over sums up her resistance well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now we move to the faster pictures. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let a few rich men run the world with no rules. I'd be at whatever protest the union called, and I'd say it loud. Online I'd probably say worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be out of work within a year. If a robot can milk, scrape, feed calves and fence, what's Femi paying me for? I've got a mortgage with nineteen years left on it and maybe six weeks of money in the bank. That's the sum, and it doesn't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't food, bills or the mortgage, straight away, and cancel the holiday to Gareth's sister's. I'd ring the bank before they ring me, to ask about a payment break. I'd go to the union for advice and I'd sign up for whatever government support exists, and I'd not be ashamed of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening. I'd be lying awake doing sums, and Gareth would be lying awake next to me, because the buses would be going too, wouldn't they?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Gareth's job. What happens at home if both of you are hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that gets me. It's not one of us losing a job, it's both of us at once, and the kids watching us panic over the kitchen table. I'd have to tell Mia not to worry when I'm worried sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it make a difference to you that this one comes so fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it changes everything. With two years nobody's ready, not the government, not the bank, not us. I'd just be grabbing for whatever's there.

S2.say: She'd call it what happens when a few rich men run the world with no rules. She'd be at any union protest and say it loudly, and worse online.
S2.think: She thinks she'd be out of work within a year, with a mortgage of nineteen years and about six weeks of savings. The sums don't add up.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except food, bills and the mortgage and cancels a family holiday. Calls the bank about a payment break, joins union protests and applies for any government support without shame.
S2.feel: Frightened and sleepless, knowing her partner's bus job would be at risk too.
S2.quote: It's not one of us losing a job, it's both of us at once, and the kids watching us panic over the kitchen table.
S2.fieldNote: Two years gives her no room, and the fear is doubled because her partner's job as a bus driver would go at the same time. She leans on the union and the state without hesitation, which fits her views. The picture of the kids watching them at the kitchen table was her most vivid moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd be on at the union to make it the main thing at every meeting. And I'd tell anyone who'd listen to vote for whoever promises a proper safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would get me to forty-eight, and I'd still have most of the mortgage. I don't think I'd be any harder to replace in five years than I am now, if I'm honest. But at least I'd see it coming this time, which I didn't with the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to pay the credit card off and get three months saved, maybe four, by doing extra Sunday shifts at calving time. I'd go door to door for the union if they ran a campaign for a guaranteed income, or for a law that farms keep people on. I'd not do a course in computers, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a steadier sort. It's like seeing a storm on the hills: you've got time to get the washing in, but it's still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see it coming this time. What's the difference between that and the school job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the school kitchen I got a letter on a Friday. This time I'd have five years of watching the letter get written. That's better and worse. Better because I can save. Worse because I'd be dreading it the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would use five years to learn the new machines. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth would tell you I go stubborn when I'm scared, and he'd be right. I'd rather fight for a rule that keeps people on than learn to babysit a robot. Maybe that's daft, but at least I'd be fighting for everyone and not just me.

S3.say: She'd say five years leaves the government no excuse for not having a plan. She'd push the union to make it the main issue and urge people to vote for a proper safety net.
S3.think: At 48 she'd be no harder to replace than she is now and still have most of the mortgage. The one comfort is seeing it coming this time.
S3.do: Pays off the credit card and builds three or four months of savings over two years with extra Sunday shifts at calving time. Campaigns door to door for the union for a guaranteed income or a law to keep people on, and turns down computer courses.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, like seeing a storm on the hills with time to get the washing in.
S3.quote: With the school kitchen I got a letter on a Friday. This time I'd have five years of watching the letter get written.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn her panic into a plan: save, then campaign. She still refuses to retrain and admits she 'goes stubborn' when scared. The contrast between a Friday letter and five years of watching it being written captures how warning time cuts both ways for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to get it right, so if they get it wrong it's on purpose. I'd want it in every manifesto. I'd say that at work and I'd say it at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'll be fifty-three, and Mia and Tom will be grown or nearly. So the worst of it lands after they've left home, which helps. But fifty-three with no job and the last few years of a mortgage, that still frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the mortgage overpaid as much as possible, even fifty a month extra, so it's smaller when it lands. I'd keep my head down at Ridgeway, get good at the job, and keep campaigning for the union. I'd wait and see what the government actually offers before I'd move or retrain, because I've been sold courses before that led nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more like a background worry than a fire. Ten years is long enough that I'd probably forget about it for weeks at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mia and Tom about their own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia wants to be a vet. I'd tell her to go for it but to make sure it's a job where people still want a person, like with the animals and the owners. I'd say, love, the robots can hold the needle, but someone's still got to hold the dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does more time make you feel better about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's what bothers me. A decade lets everyone tell themselves it's someone else's problem. Five years would make people move, ten years makes people lazy.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is plenty of time to get it right, so getting it wrong would be deliberate. She'd want it in every manifesto and say so at work and at the school gate.
S4.think: The worst would land after her children have left home, which helps. But being 53 with no job and the last of a mortgage still frightens her.
S4.do: Overpays the mortgage by about fifty a month to shrink it before AGI arrives. Stays at Ridgeway getting better at the job, keeps campaigning with the union, and waits to see what the government offers before moving or retraining.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but as a background worry rather than a fire; she'd forget about it for weeks at a time.
S4.quote: I'd say, love, the robots can hold the needle, but someone's still got to hold the dog.
S4.fieldNote: Surprisingly, Uma doesn't find ten years comforting: she thinks a long runway makes people lazy, and her own plan leans towards waiting. Her advice to her daughter about holding the dog shows she does think about where people will still be wanted. Her distrust of retraining comes from courses that led nowhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because there's no time and it hits Gareth and me together. What would help is a law that says you can't just swap people for machines overnight, a year's notice at least, and money for families while they sort themselves out. And a union that's in the room when the farm decides, not reading about it after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about us and the robots, but the animals know who handles them. I've got one old cow, number 212, who won't let down her milk unless I'm the one stood there talking to her. I'd like to think that counts for something, though I'm not daft enough to think it'll save me.

headlineQuote: I've got one old cow, number 212, who won't let down her milk unless I'm the one stood there talking to her.
portrait: Uma Evans is 43, a newer hand on a dairy and barley farm who came to farming three years ago after her school kitchen job was outsourced. She's progressive, a union member, and openly slow to learn new things; she has never used an AI tool and doesn't want to. In the mild pictures she's calm or uneasy and angry mostly at supermarkets and milk prices. When AGI arrives in 2 years she's alarmed because her partner's bus job would go too, and with more warning she saves and campaigns rather than retrains. She trusts collective action more than courses, and her strongest bond at work is with the animals.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to prepare and both she and her partner would lose their jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: A law against replacing people with machines overnight, with at least a year's notice, money for families while they adjust, and a union in the room when farms decide.
